| *(didascalia)* | Enter [[characters/belarius\|Belarius]], followed by [[characters/guiderius\|Guiderius]] and [[characters/arviragus\|Arviragus]], from a [[motifs/cave\|cave]] in the woods |
| [[characters/belarius\|BELARIUS]] | A goodly day not to keep house with such<br>Whose roof’s as low as ours. Stoop, boys; this gate<br>Instructs you how t‘adore the heavens, and bows you<br>To a morning’s holy office. The gates of monarchs<br>Are arched so high that giants may jet through<br>And keep their impious turbans on without<br>Good morrow to the sun. Hail, thou fair heaven!<br>We house i’th’ rock, yet use thee not so hardly<br>As prouder livers do. |
| [[characters/guiderius\|GUIDERIUS]] | Hail, heaven! |
| [[characters/arviragus\|ARVIRAGUS]] | Hail, heaven! |
| [[characters/belarius\|BELARIUS]] | Now for our mountain sport. Up to yon [[motifs/hill\|hill]],<br>Your legs are young; I’ll tread these flats. Consider,<br>When you above perceive me like a crow,<br>That it is place which lessens and sets off,<br>And you may then revolve what tales I have told you<br>Of courts, of princes, of the tricks in war;<br>That service is not service, so being done,<br>But being so allowed. To apprehend thus<br>Draws us a profit from all things we see,<br>And often to our comfort shall we find<br>The sharded beetle in a safer hold<br>Than is the full-winged eagle. O, this life<br>Is nobler than attending for a check,<br>Richer than doing nothing for a bauble,<br>Prouder than rustling in unpaid-for silk;<br>Such gain the cap of him that makes ’em fine,<br>Yet keeps his book uncrossed. No life to ours. |
| [[characters/guiderius\|GUIDERIUS]] | Out of your proof you speak. We, poor unfledged,<br>Have never winged from view o’th’ nest, nor know<br>not<br>What air’s from [[motifs/home\|home]]. Haply this life is best,<br>If quiet life be best; sweeter to you<br>That have a sharper known; [[motifs/well\|well]] corresponding<br>With your stiff age, but unto us it is<br>A cell of ignorance, travelling abed,<br>A [[motifs/prison\|prison]] for a debtor, that not dares<br>To stride a limit. |
| [[characters/arviragus\|ARVIRAGUS]] | (to [[characters/belarius\|Belarius]]) What should we speak of<br>When we are old as you? When we shall hear<br>The rain and [[motifs/wind\|wind]] beat dark December, how,<br>In this our pinching [[motifs/cave\|cave]], shall we discourse<br>The freezing hours away? We have seen nothing.<br>We are beastly: subtle as the fox for prey,<br>Like warlike as the wolf for what we eat.<br>Our valour is to chase what flies; our cage<br>We make a choir, as doth the prisoned bird,<br>And sing our bondage freely. |
| [[characters/belarius\|BELARIUS]] | How you speak!<br>Did you but know the [[motifs/city\|city]]’s usuries,<br>And felt them knowingly; the art o‘th’ [[settings/court\|court]],<br>As hard to leave as keep, whose top to climb<br>Is certain falling, or so slipp’ry that<br>The [[concepts/fear\|fear]]’s as bad as falling; the toil o‘th’ war,<br>A [[motifs/pain\|pain]] that only seems to seek out danger<br>I’th’ name of fame and [[concepts/honour\|honour]], which dies i‘th’ search<br>And hath as oft a sland’rous epitaph<br>As record of fair act; nay, many times<br>Doth ill deserve by doing [[motifs/well\|well]]; what’s worse,<br>Must curtsy at the censure. O boys, this story<br>The world may read in me. My [[concepts/body\|body]]’s marked<br>With Roman swords, and my report was once<br>First with the best of note. [[characters/cymbeline\|Cymbeline]] loved me,<br>And when a soldier was the theme my name<br>Was not far off. Then was I as a tree<br>Whose boughs did bend with fruit; but in one [[motifs/night\|night]]<br>A [[motifs/storm\|storm]] or robbery, call it what you will,<br>Shook down my mellow hangings, nay, my [[motifs/leaves\|leaves]],<br>And left me bare to weather. |
| [[characters/guiderius\|GUIDERIUS]] | Uncertain favour! |
| [[characters/belarius\|BELARIUS]] | My fault being nothing, as I have told you oft,<br>But that two villains, whose false oaths prevailed<br>Before my perfect [[concepts/honour\|honour]], swore to [[characters/cymbeline\|Cymbeline]]<br>I was confederate with the Romans. So<br>Followed my banishment, and this twenty years<br>This rock and these demesnes have been my world,<br>Where I have lived at honest [[concepts/freedom\|freedom]], paid<br>More pious debts to heaven than in all<br>The fore-end of my [[motifs/time\|time]]. But up to th’ [[settings/mountains\|mountains]]!<br>This is not hunter’s language. He that strikes<br>The venison first shall be the lord o’th’ feast,<br>To him the other two shall minister,<br>And we will [[concepts/fear\|fear]] no [[motifs/poison\|poison]] which attends<br>In place of greater state. I’ll meet you in the valleys. |
| *(didascalia)* | Exeunt [[characters/guiderius\|Guiderius]] and [[characters/arviragus\|Arviragus]] |
| [[characters/belarius\|BELARIUS]] | How hard it is to hide the sparks of [[concepts/nature\|nature]]!<br>These boys know little they are sons to th’ [[archetypes/king\|King]],<br>Nor [[characters/cymbeline\|Cymbeline]] [[motifs/dreams\|dreams]] that they are alive.<br>They think they are mine, and though trained up<br>thus meanly<br>I‘th’ [[motifs/cave\|cave]] wherein they bow, their thoughts do hit<br>The roofs of palaces, and [[concepts/nature\|nature]] prompts them<br>In simple and low things to prince it much<br>Beyond the trick of others. This Polydore,<br>The heir of [[characters/cymbeline\|Cymbeline]] and Britain, who<br>The [[archetypes/king\|King]] his father called [[characters/guiderius\|Guiderius]]—Jove,<br>When on my three-foot stool I sit and tell<br>The warlike feats I have done, his spirits fly out<br>Into my story: say ‘Thus mine enemy fell,<br>And thus I set my foot on ’s neck’, even then<br>The princely [[motifs/blood\|blood]] flows in his cheek, he sweats,<br>Strains his young nerves, and puts himself in posture<br>That acts my words. The younger brother, Cadwal,<br>Once [[characters/arviragus\|Arviragus]], in as like a figure<br>Strikes life into my speech, and shows much more<br>His own conceiving. |
| *(didascalia)* | A hunting-horn sounds |
| [[characters/belarius\|BELARIUS]] | Hark, the game is roused!<br>O [[characters/cymbeline\|Cymbeline]], heaven and my [[concepts/conscience\|conscience]] knows<br>Thou didst unjustly banish me, whereon<br>At three and two years old I stole these babes,<br>Thinking to bar thee of succession as<br>Thou reft’st me of my lands. Euriphile,<br>Thou wast their [[characters/nurse\|nurse]]; they took thee for their<br>mother,<br>And every day do [[concepts/honour\|honour]] to her [[motifs/grave\|grave]].<br>Myself, [[characters/belarius\|Belarius]], that am Morgan called,<br>They take for natural father. |
| *(didascalia)* | A hunting-horn sounds |
| [[characters/belarius\|BELARIUS]] | The game is up. |
| *(didascalia)* | Exit |


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

| Chi parla | Battuta |
|---|---|
| *(didascalia)* | Entra [[characters/belarius\|Belario]], seguito da [[characters/guiderius\|Guiderio]] e [[characters/arviragus\|Arvirago]], da una [[motifs/cave\|grotta]] nel bosco |
| [[characters/belarius\|BELARIO]] | Bel giorno, per non restare in casa con tali<br>che han tetto basso come il nostro. Piegatevi, ragazzi; questa porta<br>v'insegna ad adorare i cieli, e vi china<br>al santo ufficio del mattino. Le porte dei monarchi<br>son così alte d'arco che i giganti vi passano impettiti<br>e tengono i loro turbani empi senza<br>augurare il buongiorno al sole. Salve, o bel cielo!<br>Noi abitiamo nella roccia, eppure non ti trattiamo duramente<br>come fanno i più superbi viventi. |
| [[characters/guiderius\|GUIDERIO]] | Salve, cielo! |
| [[characters/arviragus\|ARVIRAGO]] | Salve, cielo! |
| [[characters/belarius\|BELARIO]] | Ora al nostro sport di montagna. Su per quel [[motifs/hill\|colle]],<br>le vostre gambe son giovani; io calcherò questi piani. Considerate:<br>quando lassù mi scorgerete simile a un corvo,<br>è il luogo che rimpicciolisce e insieme risalta,<br>e allora potrete riandare con la mente alle storie che v'ho detto<br>di corti, di principi, degli inganni della guerra;<br>che il servizio non è servizio per come vien fatto,<br>ma per come vien gradito. Comprendere così<br>ci trae profitto da ogni cosa che vediamo,<br>e spesso, a nostro conforto, troveremo<br>lo scarabeo stercorario in un riparo più sicuro<br>di quanto non sia l'aquila dall'ali spiegate. O, questa vita<br>è più nobile che servire per un rimprovero,<br>più ricca che non far nulla per un gingillo,<br>più superba che frusciare in seta non pagata;<br>costoro ottengono l'inchino di chi li fa belli,<br>ma il suo libro resta senza cancellature. Nessuna vita è pari alla nostra. |
| [[characters/guiderius\|GUIDERIO]] | Parlate per esperienza. Noi, poveri implumi,<br>non abbiamo mai spiegato le ali fuor di vista del nido, né sappiamo<br>non<br>quale aria venga da [[motifs/home\|casa]]. Forse questa vita è la migliore,<br>se la vita quieta è la migliore; più dolce a voi<br>che ne conoscete una più aspra; [[motifs/well\|ben]] rispondente<br>alla vostra rigida età, ma per noi essa è<br>una cella d'ignoranza, un viaggiare a letto,<br>una [[motifs/prison\|prigione]] per un debitore che non osa<br>varcare un limite. |
| [[characters/arviragus\|ARVIRAGO]] | (a [[characters/belarius\|Belario]]) Di che cosa parleremo<br>quando saremo vecchi come voi? Quando udremo<br>la pioggia e il [[motifs/wind\|vento]] battere il cupo dicembre, come,<br>in questa nostra [[motifs/cave\|grotta]] che ci serra, discorrendo<br>trascorreremo le ore gelide? Noi non abbiamo visto nulla.<br>Siamo bestiali: astuti come la volpe per la preda,<br>bellicosi come il lupo per ciò che mangiamo.<br>Il nostro valore è inseguire ciò che fugge; la nostra gabbia<br>facciamo un coro, come fa l'uccello prigioniero,<br>e cantiamo liberamente la nostra schiavitù. |
| [[characters/belarius\|BELARIO]] | Come parlate!<br>Se solo conosceste le usure della [[motifs/city\|città]],<br>e le sentiste per esperienza; l'arte della [[settings/court\|corte]],<br>dura a lasciare quanto a serbare, la cui cima a scalare<br>è caduta certa, o così sdrucciolevole che<br>il [[concepts/fear\|timore]] è grave quanto la caduta; la fatica della guerra,<br>un [[motifs/pain\|dolore]] che sembra cercare il pericolo soltanto<br>in nome della fama e dell'[[concepts/honour\|onore]], che muore nella ricerca<br>e ha altrettanto spesso un epitaffio infamante<br>quanto il ricordo di una bella impresa; anzi, molte volte<br>vien mal ripagato facendo il [[motifs/well\|bene]]; e, quel ch'è peggio,<br>deve inchinarsi al biasimo. O ragazzi, questa storia<br>il mondo può leggerla in me. Il mio [[concepts/body\|corpo]] è segnato<br>da spade romane, e la mia fama un tempo fu<br>la prima tra le più note. [[characters/cymbeline\|Cimbelino]] mi amò,<br>e quando il tema era un soldato, il mio nome<br>non era lontano. Allora ero come un albero<br>i cui rami piegavano di frutti; ma in una [[motifs/night\|notte]]<br>una [[motifs/storm\|tempesta]] o un furto, chiamatelo come volete,<br>scosse giù le mie mature pendenze, anzi le mie [[motifs/leaves\|foglie]],<br>e mi lasciò nudo alle intemperie. |
| [[characters/guiderius\|GUIDERIO]] | Favore incerto! |
| [[characters/belarius\|BELARIO]] | La mia colpa non essendo nulla, come spesso v'ho detto,<br>se non che due furfanti, le cui false giuramenta prevalsero<br>sul mio perfetto [[concepts/honour\|onore]], giurarono a [[characters/cymbeline\|Cimbelino]]<br>ch'ero confederato con i Romani. Così<br>seguì il mio bando, e questi vent'anni<br>questa roccia e questi domini sono stati il mio mondo,<br>dove ho vissuto in onesta [[concepts/freedom\|libertà]], pagando<br>più devoti debiti al cielo che non in tutta<br>la prima parte del mio [[motifs/time\|tempo]]. Ma su per i [[settings/mountains\|monti]]!<br>Questo non è linguaggio da cacciatore. Chi colpisce<br>per primo il cervo sarà signore del convito,<br>a lui gli altri due serviranno,<br>e noi non [[concepts/fear\|temeremo]] alcun [[motifs/poison\|veleno]] che accompagni<br>i luoghi di maggior fasto. Vi aspetterò nelle valli. |
| *(didascalia)* | Escono [[characters/guiderius\|Guiderio]] e [[characters/arviragus\|Arvirago]] |
| [[characters/belarius\|BELARIO]] | Come è difficile nascondere le scintille della [[concepts/nature\|natura]]!<br>Questi ragazzi non sanno di essere figli del [[archetypes/king\|re]],<br>né [[characters/cymbeline\|Cimbelino]] [[motifs/dreams\|sogna]] che siano vivi.<br>Credono di essere miei, e sebbene allevati<br>così umilmente<br>nella [[motifs/cave\|grotta]] dove s'inchinano, i lor pensieri battono<br>i tetti dei palazzi, e la [[concepts/nature\|natura]] li spinge<br>nelle cose semplici e basse a fare i principi<br>ben oltre l'arte degli altri. Questo Polidoro,<br>erede di [[characters/cymbeline\|Cimbelino]] e di Britannia, che<br>il [[archetypes/king\|re]] suo padre chiamò [[characters/guiderius\|Guiderio]]—Giove,<br>quando sul mio sgabello a tre gambe siedo e racconto<br>le imprese guerresche che ho compiuto, il suo spirito vola<br>dentro la mia storia: dico «Così cadde il mio nemico,<br>e così posai il piede sul suo collo», e in quel momento<br>il principesco [[motifs/blood\|sangue]] gli affluisce alla guancia, suda,<br>tende i giovani nervi, e si mette in posa<br>che rappresenta le mie parole. Il fratello minore, Cadwal,<br>già [[characters/arviragus\|Arvirago]], in figura non meno simile,<br>infonde vita al mio discorso, e mostra molto più<br>il proprio concetto. |
| *(didascalia)* | Suona un corno da caccia |
| [[characters/belarius\|BELARIO]] | Udite, la preda è scovata!<br>O [[characters/cymbeline\|Cimbelino]], il cielo e la mia [[concepts/conscience\|coscienza]] sanno<br>che ingiustamente mi bandisti; perciò<br>a tre e due anni rubai questi fanciulli,<br>pensando di precluderti la successione, come<br>tu mi togliesti le mie terre. Eurifile,<br>tu fosti la loro [[characters/nurse\|nutrice]]; essi ti presero per loro<br>madre,<br>e ogni giorno fanno [[concepts/honour\|onore]] alla sua [[motifs/grave\|tomba]].<br>Io stesso, [[characters/belarius\|Belario]], che Morgan son chiamato,<br>essi prendono per padre naturale. |
| *(didascalia)* | Suona un corno da caccia |
| [[characters/belarius\|BELARIO]] | La preda è in piedi. |
| *(didascalia)* | Esce |



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="act_3--scene_4" data-title="Cymbeline — Act III, Scene 4" data-chapter="Scene 4" data-kind="scene" data-tags="archetype/fool,archetype/innocent,archetype/king,archetype/villain,motif/clock,motif/crown,motif/death,motif/desire,motif/grave,motif/home,motif/horse,motif/lamb,motif/love,motif/memory,motif/nature,motif/night,motif/secrets,motif/silence,motif/sleep,motif/summer,motif/time,motif/well,concept/body,concept/conscience,concept/courage,concept/despair,concept/exile,concept/faith,concept/fear,concept/history,concept/honour,concept/nature,concept/revenge,concept/self,form/history,setting/court,setting/italy,character/bottom,character/cloten,character/cymbeline,character/innogen,character/lucius,character/posthumus,character/queen,character/speed"></span>


| Speaker | Line |
|---|---|
| *(didascalia)* | Enter Pisanio, and [[characters/innogen\|Innogen]] in a riding-suit |
| [[characters/innogen\|INNOGEN]] | Thou told‘st me when we came from [[motifs/horse\|horse]] the place<br>Was near at hand. Ne’er longed my mother so<br>To see me first as I have now. Pisanio, man,<br>Where is [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]]? What is in thy mind<br>That makes thee stare thus? Wherefore breaks that<br>sigh<br>From th’inward of thee? One but painted thus<br>Would be interpreted a thing perplexed<br>Beyond [[concepts/self\|self]]-explication. Put thyself<br>Into a haviour of less [[concepts/fear\|fear]], ere wildness<br>Vanquish my staider senses. What’s the matter?<br>Pisanio gives her a letter<br>Why tender‘st thou that paper to me with<br>A look untender? If’t be [[motifs/summer\|summer]] news,<br>Smile to’t before; if winterly, thou need’st<br>But keep that count’nance still. My husband’s hand?<br>That drug-damned [[settings/italy\|Italy]] hath out-craftied him,<br>And he’s at some hard point. Speak, man. Thy tongue<br>May take off some extremity which to read<br>Would be even mortal to me. |
| PISANIO | Please you read,<br>And you shall find me, wretched man, a thing<br>The most disdained of fortune. |
| [[characters/innogen\|INNOGEN]] | (reads) ‘Thy mistress, Pisanio, hath played the strumpet in my bed, the testimonies whereof lies bleeding in me. I speak not out of weak surmises but from proof as strong as my grief and as certain as I expect my [[concepts/revenge\|revenge]]. That part thou, Pisanio, must act for me, if thy [[concepts/faith\|faith]] be not tainted with the breach of hers. Let thine own hands take away her life. I shall give thee opportunity at Milford Haven. She hath my letter for the purpose, where if thou [[concepts/fear\|fear]] to strike and to make me certain it is done, thou art the pander to her dishonour and equally to me disloyal.’ |
| PISANIO | (aside)<br>What shall I need to draw my sword? The paper<br>Hath cut her throat already. No, ’tis slander,<br>Whose edge is sharper than the sword, whose tongue<br>Outvenoms all the worms of Nile, whose breath<br>Rides on the posting winds and doth belie<br>All corners of the world. Kings, queens, and states,<br>Maids, matrons, nay, the [[motifs/secrets\|secrets]] of the [[motifs/grave\|grave]]<br>This viperous slander enters. (To [[characters/innogen\|Innogen]]) What cheer,<br>madam? |
| [[characters/innogen\|INNOGEN]] | False to his bed? What is it to be false?<br>To lie in watch there and to think on him?<br>To weep ’twixt [[motifs/clock\|clock]] and [[motifs/clock\|clock]]? If [[motifs/sleep\|sleep]] charge [[concepts/nature\|nature]],<br>To break it with a fearful dream of him<br>And cry myself awake? That’s false to ’s bed, is it? |
| PISANIO | Alas, good lady. |
| [[characters/innogen\|INNOGEN]] | I false? Thy [[concepts/conscience\|conscience]] witness, Giacomo,<br>Thou didst accuse him of incontinency.<br>Thou then lookedst like a [[archetypes/villain\|villain]]; now, methinks,<br>Thy favour’s good enough. Some jay of [[settings/italy\|Italy]],<br>Whose mother was her painting, hath betrayed him.<br>Poor I am stale, a garment out of fashion,<br>And for I am richer than to hang by th’ walls<br>I must be ripped. To pieces with me! O,<br>Men’s vows are women’s traitors. All good seeming,<br>By thy revolt, O husband, shall be thought<br>Put on for villainy; not born where’t grows,<br>But worn a bait for ladies. |
| PISANIO | Good madam, hear me. |
| [[characters/innogen\|INNOGEN]] | True honest men being heard like false Aeneas<br>Were in his [[motifs/time\|time]] thought false, and Sinon’s weeping<br>Did scandal many a holy tear, took pity<br>From most true wretchedness. So thou, [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]],<br>Wilt lay the leaven on all proper men.<br>Goodly and gallant shall be false and perjured<br>From thy great fail. (To Pisanio) Come, fellow, be thou<br>honest,<br>Do thou thy master’s bidding. When thou seest<br>him,<br>A little witness my obedience. Look,<br>I draw the sword myself. Take it, and hit<br>The [[archetypes/innocent\|innocent]] mansion of my [[motifs/love\|love]], my heart.<br>[[concepts/fear\|Fear]] not, ‘tis empty of all things but grief.<br>Thy master is not there, who was indeed<br>The riches of it. Do his bidding; strike.<br>Thou mayst be valiant in a better cause,<br>But now thou seem’st a coward. |
| PISANIO | Hence, vile instrument,<br>Thou shalt not damn my hand! |
| [[characters/innogen\|INNOGEN]] | Why, I must die,<br>And if I do not by thy hand thou art<br>No servant of thy master’s. Against [[concepts/self\|self]]-slaughter<br>There is a prohibition so divine<br>That cravens my weak hand. Come, here’s my heart.<br>Something’s afore’t. Soft, soft, we’ll no defence;<br>Obedient as the scabbard. What is here?<br>She takes letters from her bosom<br>The scriptures of the loyal Leonatus,<br>All turned to heresy? Away, away,<br>Corrupters of my [[concepts/faith\|faith]], you shall no more<br>Be stomachers to my heart. Thus may poor fools<br>Believe false teachers. Though those that are betrayed<br>Do feel the treason sharply, yet the traitor<br>Stands in worse case of woe. And thou, [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]],<br>That didst set up my disobedience ’gainst the [[archetypes/king\|King]]<br>My father, and make me put into contempt the suits<br>Of princely fellows, shalt hereafter find<br>It is no act of common passage but<br>A strain of rareness; and I grieve myself<br>To think, when thou shalt be disedged by her<br>That now thou tirest on, how thy [[motifs/memory\|memory]]<br>Will then be panged by me. (To Pisanio) Prithee,<br>dispatch.<br>The [[motifs/lamb\|lamb]] entreats the butcher. Where’s thy knife?<br>Thou art too slow to do thy master’s bidding<br>When I [[motifs/desire\|desire]] it too. |
| PISANIO | O gracious lady,<br>Since I received command to do this business<br>I have not slept one wink. |
| [[characters/innogen\|INNOGEN]] | Do’t, and to bed, then. |
| PISANIO | I’ll wake mine eyeballs out first. |
| [[characters/innogen\|INNOGEN]] | Wherefore then<br>Didst undertake it? Why hast thou abused<br>So many miles with a pretence?—this place,<br>Mine action, and thine own? Our horses’ labour,<br>The [[motifs/time\|time]] inviting thee? The perturbed [[settings/court\|court]],<br>For my being absent, whereunto I never<br>Purpose return? Why hast thou gone so far<br>To be unbent when thou hast ta‘en thy stand,<br>Th’elected deer before thee? |
| PISANIO | But to win [[motifs/time\|time]]<br>To lose so bad employment, in the which<br>I have considered of a course. Good lady,<br>Hear me with patience. |
| [[characters/innogen\|INNOGEN]] | Talk thy tongue weary. Speak.<br>I have heard I am a strumpet, and mine ear,<br>Therein false struck, can take no greater wound,<br>Nor tent to [[characters/bottom\|bottom]] that. But speak. |
| PISANIO | Then, madam,<br>I thought you would not back again. |
| [[characters/innogen\|INNOGEN]] | Most like,<br>Bringing me here to kill me. |
| PISANIO | Not so, neither.<br>But if I were as wise as honest, then<br>My purpose would prove [[motifs/well\|well]]. It cannot be<br>But that my master is abused. Some [[archetypes/villain\|villain]],<br>Ay, and singular in his art, hath done you both<br>This cursed injury. |
| [[characters/innogen\|INNOGEN]] | Some Roman courtesan. |
| PISANIO | No, on my life.<br>I’ll give but notice you are dead, and send him<br>Some bloody sign of it, for ’tis commanded<br>I should do so. You shall be missed at [[settings/court\|court]],<br>And that will [[motifs/well\|well]] confirm it. |
| [[characters/innogen\|INNOGEN]] | Why, good fellow,<br>What shall I do the while, where bide, how live,<br>Or in my life what comfort when I am<br>Dead to my husband? |
| PISANIO | If you’ll back to th’ [[settings/court\|court]]— |
| [[characters/innogen\|INNOGEN]] | No [[settings/court\|court]], no father, nor no more ado<br>With that harsh, churlish, noble, simple nothing,<br>That [[characters/cloten\|Cloten]], whose [[motifs/love\|love]] suit hath been to me<br>As fearful as a siege. |
| PISANIO | If not at [[settings/court\|court]],<br>Then not in Britain must you bide. |
| [[characters/innogen\|INNOGEN]] | Where then?<br>Hath Britain all the sun that shines? Day, [[motifs/night\|night]],<br>Are they not but in Britain? I‘th’ world’s volume<br>Our Britain seems as of it but not in’t,<br>In a great pool a swan’s nest. Prithee, think<br>There’s livers out of Britain. |
| PISANIO | I am most glad<br>You think of other place. Th‘ambassador,<br>[[characters/lucius\|Lucius]] the Roman, comes to Milford Haven<br>Tomorrow. Now if you could wear a mind<br>Dark as your fortune is, and but disguise<br>That which t’appear itself must not yet be<br>But by [[concepts/self\|self]]-danger, you should tread a course<br>Pretty and full of view; yea, haply near<br>The residence of [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]]; so nigh, at least,<br>That though his actions were not visible, yet<br>Report should render him hourly to your ear<br>As truly as he moves. |
| [[characters/innogen\|INNOGEN]] | O, for such means,<br>Though peril to my modesty, not [[motifs/death\|death]] on’t,<br>I would adventure. |
| PISANIO | [[motifs/well\|Well]] then, here’s the point:<br>You must forget to be a woman; change<br>Command into obedience, [[concepts/fear\|fear]] and niceness—<br>The handmaids of all women, or more truly<br>Woman it pretty [[concepts/self\|self]]—into a waggish [[concepts/courage\|courage]],<br>Ready in gibes, quick-answered, saucy and<br>As quarrelous as the weasel. Nay, you must<br>Forget that rarest treasure of your cheek,<br>Exposing it—but O, the harder heart!—<br>Alack, no remedy—to the greedy touch<br>Of common-kissing Titan, and forget<br>Your laboursome and dainty trims wherein<br>You made great Juno angry. |
| [[characters/innogen\|INNOGEN]] | Nay, be brief.<br>I see into thy end, and am almost<br>A man already. |
| PISANIO | First, make yourself but like one.<br>Forethinking this, I have already fit—<br>’Tis in my cloak-bag—doublet, hat, hose, all<br>That answer to them. Would you in their serving,<br><br>And with what imitation you can borrow<br>From youth of such a season, fore noble [[characters/lucius\|Lucius]]<br>Present yourself, [[motifs/desire\|desire]] his service, tell him<br>Wherein you’re happy—which will make him know<br>If that his head have ear in music—doubtless<br>With joy he will embrace you, for he’s honourable,<br>And, doubling that, most holy. Your means abroad—<br>You have me, rich, and I will never fail<br>Beginning nor supplyment. |
| [[characters/innogen\|INNOGEN]] | Thou art all the comfort<br>The gods will diet me with. Prithee away.<br>There’s more to be considered, but we’ll even<br>All that good [[motifs/time\|time]] will give us. This attempt<br>I am soldier to, and will abide it with<br>A prince’s [[concepts/courage\|courage]]. Away, I prithee. |
| PISANIO | [[motifs/well\|Well]], madam, we must take a short farewell<br>Lest, being missed, I be suspected of<br>Your carriage from the [[settings/court\|court]]. My noble mistress,<br>Here is a box. I had it from the [[characters/queen\|Queen]].<br>What’s in’t is precious. If you are sick at sea<br>Or stomach-qualmed at land, a dram of this<br>Will drive away distemper. To some shade,<br>And fit you to your manhood. May the gods<br>Direct you to the best. |
| [[characters/innogen\|INNOGEN]] | Amen. I thank thee. |
| *(didascalia)* | Exeunt severally |
| *(didascalia)* | 3.5 Flourish. Enter [[characters/cymbeline\|Cymbeline]], the [[characters/queen\|Queen]], [[characters/cloten\|Cloten]], [[characters/lucius\|Lucius]], and lords |
| [[characters/cymbeline\|CYMBELINE]] | (to [[characters/lucius\|Lucius]])<br>Thus far, and so farewell. |
| [[characters/lucius\|LUCIUS]] | Thanks, royal sir.<br>My emperor hath wrote I must from hence;<br>And am right sorry that I must report ye<br>My master’s enemy. |
| [[characters/cymbeline\|CYMBELINE]] | Our subjects, sir,<br>Will not endure his yoke, and for ourself<br>To show less sovereignty than they must needs<br>Appear unkinglike. |
| [[characters/lucius\|LUCIUS]] | So, sir, I [[motifs/desire\|desire]] of you<br>A conduct over land to Milford Haven. |
| *(didascalia)* | (To the [[characters/queen\|Queen]]) Madam, all joy befall your grace, to [[characters/cloten\|Cloten]] and you. |
| [[characters/cymbeline\|CYMBELINE]] | My lords, you are appointed for that office.<br>The due of [[concepts/honour\|honour]] in no point omit.<br>So farewell, noble [[characters/lucius\|Lucius]]. |
| [[characters/lucius\|LUCIUS]] | Your hand, my lord. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Receive it friendly, but from this [[motifs/time\|time]] forth<br>I wear it as your enemy. |
| [[characters/lucius\|LUCIUS]] | Sir, the event<br>Is yet to name the winner. Fare you [[motifs/well\|well]]. |
| [[characters/cymbeline\|CYMBELINE]] | Leave not the worthy [[characters/lucius\|Lucius]], good my lords,<br>Till he have crossed the Severn. Happiness. |
| *(didascalia)* | Exeunt [[characters/lucius\|Lucius]] and lords |
| [[characters/queen\|QUEEN]] | He goes hence frowning, but it honours us<br>That we have given him cause. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | ’Tis all the better.<br>Your valiant Britons have their wishes in it. |
| [[characters/cymbeline\|CYMBELINE]] | [[characters/lucius\|Lucius]] hath wrote already to the Emperor<br>How it goes here. It fits us therefore ripely<br>Our chariots and our horsemen be in readiness.<br>The powers that he already hath in Gallia<br>Will soon be drawn to head, from whence he moves<br>His war for Britain. |
| [[characters/queen\|QUEEN]] | ’Tis not sleepy business,<br>But must be looked to speedily and strongly. |
| [[characters/cymbeline\|CYMBELINE]] | Our expectation that it would be thus<br>Hath made us forward. But, my gentle [[characters/queen\|queen]],<br>Where is our daughter? She hath not appeared<br>Before the Roman, nor to us hath tendered<br>The duty of the day. She looks us like<br>A thing more made of malice than of duty.<br>We have noted it. Call her before us, for<br>We have been too slight in sufferance. |
| *(didascalia)* | Exit one or more |
| [[characters/queen\|QUEEN]] | Royal Sir,<br>Since the [[concepts/exile\|exile]] of [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]] most retired<br>Hath her life been, the cure ,whereof, my lord,<br>’Tis [[motifs/time\|time]] must do. Beseech your majesty<br>Forbear sharp speeches to her. She’s a lady<br>So tender of rebukes that words are strokes,<br>And strokes [[motifs/death\|death]] to her. |
| *(didascalia)* | Enter a Messenger |
| [[characters/cymbeline\|CYMBELINE]] | Where is she, sir? How<br>Can her contempt be answered? |
| MESSENGER | Please you, sir,<br>Her chambers are all locked, and there’s no answer<br>That will be given to th’ loud’st of noise we make. |
| [[characters/queen\|QUEEN]] | My lord, when last I went to visit her<br>She prayed me to excuse her keeping close,<br>Whereto constrained by her infirmity,<br>She should that duty leave unpaid to you<br>Which daily she was bound to proffer. This<br>She wished me to make known, but our great<br>[[settings/court\|court]]<br>Made me to blame in [[motifs/memory\|memory]]. |
| [[characters/cymbeline\|CYMBELINE]] | Her doors locked?<br>Not seen of late? Grant heavens that which I<br>[[concepts/fear\|Fear]] prove false. |
| *(didascalia)* | Exit |
| [[characters/queen\|QUEEN]] | on, I say, follow the [[archetypes/king\|King]]. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | That man of hers, Pisanio, her old servant,<br>I have not seen these two days. |
| [[characters/queen\|QUEEN]] | Go, look after. |
| *(didascalia)* | Exit [[characters/cloten\|Cloten]] |
| [[characters/queen\|QUEEN]] | Pisanio, thou that stand’st so for [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]]!<br>He hath a drug of mine. I pray his absence<br>Proceed by swallowing that, for he believes<br>It is a thing most precious. But for her,<br>Where is she gone? Haply [[concepts/despair\|despair]] hath seized her,<br>Or, winged with fervour of her [[motifs/love\|love]], she’s flown<br>To her desired [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]]. Gone she is<br>To [[motifs/death\|death]] or to dishonour, and my end<br>Can make good use of either. She being down,<br>I have the placing of the British [[motifs/crown\|crown]]. |
| *(didascalia)* | Enter [[characters/cloten\|Cloten]] |
| [[characters/queen\|QUEEN]] | How now, my son? |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | ’Tis certain she is fled.<br>Go in and cheer the [[archetypes/king\|King]]. He rages, none<br>Dare come about him. |
| [[characters/queen\|QUEEN]] | All the better. May<br>This [[motifs/night\|night]] forestall him of the coming day. Exit |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | I [[motifs/love\|love]] and hate her. For she’s fair and royal,<br>And that she hath all courtly parts more exquisite<br>Than lady, ladies, woman—from every one<br>The best she hath, and she, of all compounded,<br>Outsells them all—I [[motifs/love\|love]] her therefore; but<br>Disdaining me, and throwing favours on<br>The low [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]], slanders so her judgement<br>That what’s else rare is choked; and in that point<br>I will conclude to hate her, nay, indeed,<br>To be revenged upon her. For when fools<br>Shall— |
| *(didascalia)* | Enter Pisanio |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Who is here? What, are you packing, sirrah?<br>Come hither. Ah, you precious pander! [[archetypes/villain\|Villain]],<br>Where is thy lady? In a word, or else<br>Thou art straightway with the fiends. |
| PISANIO | O good my lord! |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Where is thy lady?—or, by Jupiter,<br>I will not ask again. Close [[archetypes/villain\|villain]],<br>I’ll have this secret from thy tongue or rip<br>Thy heart to find it. Is she with [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]],<br>From whose so many weights of baseness cannot<br>A dram of worth be drawn? |
| PISANIO | Alas, my lord,<br>How can she be with him? When was she missed?<br>He is in Rome. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Where is she, sir? Come nearer.<br>No farther halting. Satisfy me [[motifs/home\|home]]<br>What is become of her. |
| PISANIO | O my all-worthy lord! |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | All-worthy [[archetypes/villain\|villain]],<br>Discover where thy mistress is at once,<br>At the next word. No more of ‘worthy lord’.<br>Speak, or thy [[motifs/silence\|silence]] on the instant is<br>Thy condemnation and thy [[motifs/death\|death]]. |
| PISANIO | Then, sir,<br>This paper is the [[concepts/history\|history]] of my knowledge<br>Touching her flight.<br>He gives [[characters/cloten\|Cloten]] a letter |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Let’s see’t. I will pursue her<br>Even to Augustus’ throne. |
| *(didascalia)* | PISANIO aside |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Or this or perish.<br>She’s far enough, and what he learns by this<br>May prove his travel, not her danger. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Hum! |
| PISANIO | (aside)<br>I’ll write to my lord she’s dead. O [[characters/innogen\|Innogen]],<br>Safe mayst thou wander, safe return again! |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Sirrah, is this letter true? |
| PISANIO | Sir, as I think. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | It is [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]]’ hand; I know’t. Sirrah, if thou wouldst not be a [[archetypes/villain\|villain]] but do me true service, undergo those employments wherein I should have cause to use thee with a serious industry—that is, what villainy soe’er I bid thee do, to perform it directly and truly—I would think thee an honest man. Thou shouldst neither want my means for thy relief nor my voice for thy preferment. |
| PISANIO | [[motifs/well\|Well]], my good lord. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Wilt thou serve me? For since patiently and constantly thou hast stuck to the bare fortune of that beggar [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]], thou canst not in the course of gratitude but be a diligent follower of mine. Wilt thou serve me? 121 |
| PISANIO | Sir, I will. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Give me thy hand. Here’s my purse. Hast any of thy late master’s garments in thy possession? |
| PISANIO | I have, my lord, at my lodging the same suit he wore when he took leave of my lady and mistress. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | The first service thou dost me, fetch that suit hither. Let it be thy first service. Go. |
| PISANIO | I shall, my lord. Exit |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Meet thee at Milford Haven! I forgot to ask him one thing; I’ll remember’t anon. Even there, thou [[archetypes/villain\|villain]] [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]], will I kill thee. I would these garments were come. She said upon a [[motifs/time\|time]]—the bitterness of it I now belch from my heart—that she held the very garment of [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]] in more respect than my noble and natural person, together with the adornment of my qualities. With that suit upon my back will I ravish her—first kill him, and in her eyes; there shall she see my valour, which will then be a torment to her contempt. He on the ground, my speech of insultment ended on his dead [[concepts/body\|body]], and when my lust hath dined—which, as I say, to vex her I will execute in the clothes that she so praised—to the [[settings/court\|court]] I’ll knock her back, foot her [[motifs/home\|home]] again. She hath despised me rejoicingly, and I’ll be merry in my [[concepts/revenge\|revenge]]. |
| *(didascalia)* | Enter Pisanio with [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]]’ suit |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Be those the garments? |
| PISANIO | Ay, my noble lord. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | How long is’t since she went to Milford Haven? |
| PISANIO | She can scarce be there yet. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Bring this apparel to my chamber. That is the second thing that I have commanded thee. The third is that thou wilt be a voluntary mute to my design. Be but duteous, and true preferment shall tender itself to thee. My [[concepts/revenge\|revenge]] is now at Milford. Would I had wings to follow it. Come, and be true. Exit |
| PISANIO | Thou bidd’st me to my loss, for true to thee<br>Were to prove false, which I will never be<br>To him that is most true. To Milford go,<br>And find not her whom thou pursuest. Flow, flow,<br>You heavenly blessings, on her. This [[archetypes/fool\|fool]]’s [[characters/speed\|speed]]<br>Be crossed with slowness; labour be his meed. Exit |

| *(didascalia)* | Entrano Pisanio e [[characters/innogen\|Innogen]] in abito da cavalcata |
| [[characters/innogen\|IMOGENE]] | Mi dicesti che, scendendo da [[motifs/horse\|horse]], il luogo<br>Era vicino. Mai mia madre bramò tanto<br>Di vedermi come io ora bramo. Pisanio, amico,<br>Dov'è [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]]? Che hai nella mente<br>Che ti fa fissare così? Perché quel sospiro<br>Sorge dal tuo intimo? Un uomo dipinto così<br>Sarebbe giudicato cosa perplessa<br>Oltre ogni [[concepts/self\|self]]-spiegazione. Mettiti<br>Un contegno di minor [[concepts/fear\|fear]], prima che la follia<br>Vinca i miei sensi più assennati. Che accade?<br>Pisanio le dà una lettera<br>Perché mi porgi quella carta con<br>Uno sguardo non tenero? Se è notizia [[motifs/summer\|summer]],<br>Sorridile prima; se invernale, tu devi<br>Solo mantenere quel volto. La mano di mio marito?<br>Quella [[settings/italy\|Italy]] maledetta di droghe lo ha ingannato,<br>Ed è in qualche grave frangente. Parla, amico. La tua lingua<br>Può lenire qualche estremità che, letta,<br>Mi sarebbe persino mortale. |
| PISANIO | Vi prego, leggete,<br>E mi troverete, uomo sventurato, cosa<br>La più disdegnata dalla sorte. |
| [[characters/innogen\|IMOGENE]] | (legge) «La tua padrona, Pisanio, ha fatto la meretrice nel mio letto; le testimonianze di ciò giacciono sanguinanti in me. Non parlo per deboli congetture, ma per prove forti come il mio dolore e certe come la mia attesa [[concepts/revenge\|revenge]]. Quella parte, Pisanio, devi recitare per me, se la tua [[concepts/faith\|faith]] non è macchiata dalla violazione della sua. Le tue stesse mani tolgano la sua vita. Ti darò l'occasione a Milford Haven. Ella ha la mia lettera a tale scopo, dove se tu [[concepts/fear\|fear]] di colpire e di rendermi certo che è fatto, sei il mezzano del suo disonore e ugualmente sleale verso di me.» |
| PISANIO | (a parte)<br>Che bisogno ho di sguainare la mia sword? La carta<br>Le ha già tagliato la gola. No, è calunnia,<br>Il cui filo è più affilato della sword, la cui lingua<br>Velenizza più di tutti i vermi del Nilo, il cui respiro<br>Cavalca i venti veloci e calunnia<br>Ogni angolo del mondo. Re, regine e stati,<br>Fanciulle, matrone, anzi i [[motifs/secrets\|secrets]] della [[motifs/grave\|grave]]<br>Questa vipera di calunnia penetra. (A [[characters/innogen\|Innogen]]) Come state, signora? |
| [[characters/innogen\|IMOGENE]] | Infedele al suo letto? Che cosa è essere infedele?<br>Stare lì a vegliare e pensare a lui?<br>Piangere tra un [[motifs/clock\|clock]] e l'altro? Se il [[motifs/sleep\|sleep]] grava sulla [[concepts/nature\|nature]],<br>Spezzarlo con un sogno pauroso di lui<br>E piangendo svegliarmi? Questo è essere infedele al suo letto, è così? |
| PISANIO | Ahimè, buona signora. |
| [[characters/innogen\|IMOGENE]] | Io infedele? Sia testimone la tua [[concepts/conscience\|conscience]], Giacomo,<br>Tu lo accusasti d'incontinenza.<br>Allora sembravi un [[archetypes/villain\|villain]]; ora, mi pare,<br>Il tuo aspetto è abbastanza buono. Una ghiandaia d'[[settings/italy\|Italy]],<br>La cui madre era il suo trucco, lo ha tradito.<br>Povera me, sono stantia, una veste fuori moda,<br>E poiché sono troppo ricca per restare appesa ai muri<br>Devo essere strappata. A pezzi, con me! O,<br>I voti degli uomini sono traditori delle donne. Ogni buona apparenza,<br>Per il tuo tradimento, o marito, sarà ritenuta<br>Indossata per malvagità; non nata dove cresce,<br>Ma portata come esca per le dame. |
| PISANIO | Buona signora, ascoltatemi. |
| [[characters/innogen\|IMOGENE]] | Gli uomini veramente onesti, ascoltati come il falso Enea,<br>Furono al suo [[motifs/time\|time]] ritenuti falsi, e il pianto di Sinone<br>Scosse molte lacrime sante, tolse pietà<br>Alla più vera miseria. Così tu, [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]],<br>Getterai il lievito su tutti gli uomini onesti.<br>Il bello e il galante saranno falsi e spergiuri<br>Per la tua grande caduta. (A Pisanio) Vieni, amico, sii onesto,<br>Fa' il volere del tuo padrone. Quando lo vedrai,<br>Sii un po' testimone della mia obbedienza. Guarda,<br>Io stessa sguaino la sword. Prendila, e colpisci<br>La [[archetypes/innocent\|innocent]] dimora del mio [[motifs/love\|love]], il mio cuore.<br>Non [[concepts/fear\|fear]], è vuoto di ogni cosa tranne il dolore.<br>Il tuo padrone non è lì, che era in verità<br>La sua ricchezza. Fa' il suo volere; colpisci.<br>Puoi essere valoroso in una causa migliore,<br>Ma ora sembri un codardo. |
| PISANIO | Via, vile strumento,<br>Non dannare la mia mano! |

Contro il [[concepts/self\|self]]-suicidio<br>C'è un divieto così divino<br>Che rende codarda la mia debole mano. Vieni, ecco il mio cuore.<br>Qualcosa è davanti. Piano, piano, non faremo difesa;<br>Obbediente come il fodero. Che c'è qui?<br>Estrae lettere dal petto<br>Le scritture del leale Leonato,<br>Tutte mutate in eresia? Via, via,<br>Corruttori della mia [[concepts/faith\|faith]], non sarete più<br>Pettorali del mio cuore. Così i poveri sciocchi<br>Credono a falsi maestri. Sebbene i traditi<br>Sentano acuto il tradimento, il traditore<br>Si trova in peggiore stato di dolore. E tu, [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]],<br>Che hai suscitato la mia disobbedienza contro il [[archetypes/king\|King]]<br>Mio padre, e mi hai fatto disprezzare le proposte<br>Di principeschi pretendenti, d'ora in poi troverai<br>Che non è atto comune, ma<br>Un tratto di rarità; e mi dolgo<br>Nel pensare che, quando sarai stuccato da colei<br>Di cui ora ti sazi, come la tua [[motifs/memory\|memory]]<br>Sarà allora tormentata da me. (A Pisanio) Ti prego, sbrigati.<br>L'[[motifs/lamb\|lamb]] prega il macellaio. | PISANIO | Prima mi caverò gli occhi. |

Perché sei giunto così lontano<br>Per non scoccare quando hai preso posizione,<br>Con il cervo eletto davanti a te? |

| [[characters/innogen\|IMOGENE]] | Parla finché la lingua si stanchi. Parla.<br>Ho sentito che sono una meretrice, e il mio orecchio,<br>Colpito falsamente, non può ricevere ferita maggiore,<br>Né sonda per giungere al [[characters/bottom\|bottom]] di ciò. Ma parla. |

| *(didascalia)* | Entra Pisanio |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Chi è qui? Che, te ne vai, furfante?<br>Vieni qua. Ah, prezioso mezzano! [[archetypes/villain\|Villain]],<br>Dov'è la tua padrona? In una parola, o altrimenti<br>Sei subito con i diavoli. |
| PISANIO | O buon mio signore! |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Dov'è la tua padrona?—o, per Giove,<br>Non lo chiederò di nuovo. Rinchiuso [[archetypes/villain\|villain]],<br>Avrò questo segreto dalla tua lingua o squarcerò<br>Il tuo cuore per trovarlo. È con [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]],<br>Dalle cui tante libbre di bassezza non può<br>Essere tratto un dramma di valore? |
| PISANIO | Ahimè, mio signore,<br>Come può essere con lui? Quando è stata vista mancare?<br>Lui è a Roma. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Dov'è, signore? Avvicinati.<br>Niente più esitazioni. Soddisfami [[motifs/home\|home]]<br>Che ne è stato di lei. |
| PISANIO | O mio signore degno di tutto! |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Degno di tutto [[archetypes/villain\|villain]],<br>Scopri dov'è la tua padrona subito,<br>Alla prossima parola. Basta con 'degno signore'.<br>Parla, o il tuo [[motifs/silence\|silence]] all'istante è<br>La tua condanna e la tua [[motifs/death\|death]]. |
| PISANIO | Allora, signore,<br>Questa carta è la [[concepts/history\|history]] di quanto so<br>Riguardo alla sua fuga.<br>Dà a [[characters/cloten\|Cloten]] una lettera |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Vediamo. La inseguirò<br>Fino al trono di Augusto. |
| *(didascalia)* | PISANIO a parte |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | O questo o perire.<br>Lei è abbastanza lontana, e ciò che lui apprende da questo<br>Può essere il suo viaggio, non il pericolo di lei. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Uhm! |
| PISANIO | (a parte)<br>Scriverò al mio signore che è morta. O [[characters/innogen\|Innogen]],<br>Possa tu vagare sicura, sicura tornare ancora! |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Furfante, è vera questa lettera? |
| PISANIO | Signore, credo di sì. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | È la mano di [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]]; la conosco. Furfante, se tu non volessi essere un [[archetypes/villain\|villain]] ma rendermi vero servizio, affrontare quegli impieghi in cui avrei motivo di usarti con seria industria—cioè, qualunque malvagità io ti ordini di fare, eseguirla direttamente e sinceramente—ti riterrei un uomo onesto. Non ti mancherebbero i miei mezzi per il tuo sostentamento né la mia voce per la tua promozione. |
| PISANIO | [[motifs/well\|Well]], mio buon signore. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Vuoi servirmi? Poiché con pazienza e costanza ti sei attaccato alla nuda fortuna di quel mendicante [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]], non puoi nel corso della gratitudine che essere un diligente seguace mio. Vuoi servirmi? 121 |
| PISANIO | Signore, lo farò. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Dammi la mano. Ecco la mia borsa. Hai qualcuno dei vestiti del tuo defunto padrone in tuo possesso? |
| PISANIO | Ne ho, mio signore, nel mio alloggio lo stesso abito che indossava quando prese congedo dalla mia signora e padrona. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Il primo servizio che mi fai, porta qui quell'abito. Sia il tuo primo servizio. Va'. |
| PISANIO | Lo farò, mio signore. Esce |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Ti incontrerò a Milford Haven! Ho dimenticato di chiedergli una cosa; me ne ricorderò tra poco. Anche lì, [[archetypes/villain\|villain]] [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]], ti ucciderò. Vorrei che quei vestiti fossero arrivati. Ella disse una volta—l'amarezza ora la ruggisco dal cuore—che teneva lo stesso abito di [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]] in maggior rispetto della mia nobile e naturale persona, insieme all'ornamento delle mie qualità. Con quell'abito sulle spalle la violento—prima uccido lui, e davanti ai suoi occhi; lì vedrà il mio valore, che sarà allora un tormento per il suo disprezzo. Lui al suolo, finito il mio discorso d'insulto sul suo morto [[concepts/body\|body]], e quando la mia lussuria avrà cenato—che, come dico, per tormentarla eseguirò nei vestiti che tanto lodò—a [[settings/court\|court]] la ricaccerò, la riporterò a [[motifs/home\|home]] a calci. Ella mi ha disprezzato con gioia, e io sarò allegro nella mia [[concepts/revenge\|revenge]]. |
| *(didascalia)* | Entra Pisanio con l'abito di [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]] |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Sono quelli i vestiti? |
| PISANIO | Sì, mio nobile signore. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Quanto tempo è passato da quando è andata a Milford Haven? |
| PISANIO | Non può ancora esserci. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Porta questi abiti nella mia camera. Questa è la seconda cosa che ti ho comandato. La terza è che sarai un muto volontario al mio disegno. Sii solo ubbidiente, e il vero avanzamento ti si offrirà da sé. La mia [[concepts/revenge\|revenge]] è ora a Milford. Vorrei avere ali per seguirla. Vieni, e sii fedele. Esce |
| PISANIO | Tu mi comandi la mia rovina, perché esser vero a te<br>Sarebbe provarsi falso, cosa che non sarò mai<br>A colui che è il più vero. A Milford va',<br>E non trovare colei che insegui. Scorrano, scorrano,<br>Le celesti benedizioni su di lei. Questo [[archetypes/fool\|fool]]'s [[characters/speed\|speed]]<br>Sia incrociato con lentezza; la fatica sia il suo premio. Esce |



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="act_3--scene_5" data-title="Cymbeline — Act III, Scene 5" data-chapter="Scene 5" data-kind="scene" data-tags="archetype/fool,archetype/king,archetype/villain,motif/crown,motif/death,motif/desire,motif/home,motif/love,motif/memory,motif/night,motif/silence,motif/time,motif/well,concept/body,concept/despair,concept/exile,concept/fear,concept/history,concept/honour,concept/revenge,form/history,setting/court,character/cloten,character/cymbeline,character/innogen,character/lucius,character/posthumus,character/queen,character/speed"></span>


| Speaker | Line |
|---|---|
| *(didascalia)* | Flourish. Enter [[characters/cymbeline\|Cymbeline]], the [[characters/queen\|Queen]], [[characters/cloten\|Cloten]], [[characters/lucius\|Lucius]], and lords |
| [[characters/cymbeline\|CYMBELINE]] | (to [[characters/lucius\|Lucius]])<br>Thus far, and so farewell. |
| [[characters/lucius\|LUCIUS]] | Thanks, royal sir.<br>My emperor hath wrote I must from hence;<br>And am right sorry that I must report ye<br>My master’s enemy. |
| [[characters/cymbeline\|CYMBELINE]] | Our subjects, sir,<br>Will not endure his yoke, and for ourself<br>To show less sovereignty than they must needs<br>Appear unkinglike. |
| [[characters/lucius\|LUCIUS]] | So, sir, I [[motifs/desire\|desire]] of you<br>A conduct over land to Milford Haven. |
| *(didascalia)* | (To the [[characters/queen\|Queen]]) Madam, all joy befall your grace, to [[characters/cloten\|Cloten]] and you. |
| [[characters/cymbeline\|CYMBELINE]] | My lords, you are appointed for that office.<br>The due of [[concepts/honour\|honour]] in no point omit.<br>So farewell, noble [[characters/lucius\|Lucius]]. |
| [[characters/lucius\|LUCIUS]] | Your hand, my lord. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Receive it friendly, but from this [[motifs/time\|time]] forth<br>I wear it as your enemy. |
| [[characters/lucius\|LUCIUS]] | Sir, the event<br>Is yet to name the winner. Fare you [[motifs/well\|well]]. |
| [[characters/cymbeline\|CYMBELINE]] | Leave not the worthy [[characters/lucius\|Lucius]], good my lords,<br>Till he have crossed the Severn. Happiness. |
| *(didascalia)* | Exeunt [[characters/lucius\|Lucius]] and lords |
| [[characters/queen\|QUEEN]] | He goes hence frowning, but it honours us<br>That we have given him cause. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | ’Tis all the better.<br>Your valiant Britons have their wishes in it. |
| [[characters/cymbeline\|CYMBELINE]] | [[characters/lucius\|Lucius]] hath wrote already to the Emperor<br>How it goes here. It fits us therefore ripely<br>Our chariots and our horsemen be in readiness.<br>The powers that he already hath in Gallia<br>Will soon be drawn to head, from whence he moves<br>His war for Britain. |
| [[characters/queen\|QUEEN]] | ’Tis not sleepy business,<br>But must be looked to speedily and strongly. |
| [[characters/cymbeline\|CYMBELINE]] | Our expectation that it would be thus<br>Hath made us forward. But, my gentle [[characters/queen\|queen]],<br>Where is our daughter? She hath not appeared<br>Before the Roman, nor to us hath tendered<br>The duty of the day. She looks us like<br>A thing more made of malice than of duty.<br>We have noted it. Call her before us, for<br>We have been too slight in sufferance. |
| *(didascalia)* | Exit one or more |
| [[characters/queen\|QUEEN]] | Royal Sir,<br>Since the [[concepts/exile\|exile]] of [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]] most retired<br>Hath her life been, the cure ,whereof, my lord,<br>’Tis [[motifs/time\|time]] must do. Beseech your majesty<br>Forbear sharp speeches to her. She’s a lady<br>So tender of rebukes that words are strokes,<br>And strokes [[motifs/death\|death]] to her. |
| *(didascalia)* | Enter a Messenger |
| [[characters/cymbeline\|CYMBELINE]] | Where is she, sir? How<br>Can her contempt be answered? |
| MESSENGER | Please you, sir,<br>Her chambers are all locked, and there’s no answer<br>That will be given to th’ loud’st of noise we make. |
| [[characters/queen\|QUEEN]] | My lord, when last I went to visit her<br>She prayed me to excuse her keeping close,<br>Whereto constrained by her infirmity,<br>She should that duty leave unpaid to you<br>Which daily she was bound to proffer. This<br>She wished me to make known, but our great<br>[[settings/court\|court]]<br>Made me to blame in [[motifs/memory\|memory]]. |
| [[characters/cymbeline\|CYMBELINE]] | Her doors locked?<br>Not seen of late? Grant heavens that which I<br>[[concepts/fear\|Fear]] prove false. |
| *(didascalia)* | Exit |
| [[characters/queen\|QUEEN]] | on, I say, follow the [[archetypes/king\|King]]. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | That man of hers, Pisanio, her old servant,<br>I have not seen these two days. |
| [[characters/queen\|QUEEN]] | Go, look after. |
| *(didascalia)* | Exit [[characters/cloten\|Cloten]] |
| [[characters/queen\|QUEEN]] | Pisanio, thou that stand’st so for [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]]!<br>He hath a drug of mine. I pray his absence<br>Proceed by swallowing that, for he believes<br>It is a thing most precious. But for her,<br>Where is she gone? Haply [[concepts/despair\|despair]] hath seized her,<br>Or, winged with fervour of her [[motifs/love\|love]], she’s flown<br>To her desired [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]]. Gone she is<br>To [[motifs/death\|death]] or to dishonour, and my end<br>Can make good use of either. She being down,<br>I have the placing of the British [[motifs/crown\|crown]]. |
| *(didascalia)* | Enter [[characters/cloten\|Cloten]] |
| [[characters/queen\|QUEEN]] | How now, my son? |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | ’Tis certain she is fled.<br>Go in and cheer the [[archetypes/king\|King]]. He rages, none<br>Dare come about him. |
| [[characters/queen\|QUEEN]] | All the better. May<br>This [[motifs/night\|night]] forestall him of the coming day. Exit |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | I [[motifs/love\|love]] and hate her. For she’s fair and royal,<br>And that she hath all courtly parts more exquisite<br>Than lady, ladies, woman—from every one<br>The best she hath, and she, of all compounded,<br>Outsells them all—I [[motifs/love\|love]] her therefore; but<br>Disdaining me, and throwing favours on<br>The low [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]], slanders so her judgement<br>That what’s else rare is choked; and in that point<br>I will conclude to hate her, nay, indeed,<br>To be revenged upon her. For when fools<br>Shall— |
| *(didascalia)* | Enter Pisanio |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Who is here? What, are you packing, sirrah?<br>Come hither. Ah, you precious pander! [[archetypes/villain\|Villain]],<br>Where is thy lady? In a word, or else<br>Thou art straightway with the fiends. |
| PISANIO | O good my lord! |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Where is thy lady?—or, by Jupiter,<br>I will not ask again. Close [[archetypes/villain\|villain]],<br>I’ll have this secret from thy tongue or rip<br>Thy heart to find it. Is she with [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]],<br>From whose so many weights of baseness cannot<br>A dram of worth be drawn? |
| PISANIO | Alas, my lord,<br>How can she be with him? When was she missed?<br>He is in Rome. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Where is she, sir? Come nearer.<br>No farther halting. Satisfy me [[motifs/home\|home]]<br>What is become of her. |
| PISANIO | O my all-worthy lord! |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | All-worthy [[archetypes/villain\|villain]],<br>Discover where thy mistress is at once,<br>At the next word. No more of ‘worthy lord’.<br>Speak, or thy [[motifs/silence\|silence]] on the instant is<br>Thy condemnation and thy [[motifs/death\|death]]. |
| PISANIO | Then, sir,<br>This paper is the [[concepts/history\|history]] of my knowledge<br>Touching her flight.<br>He gives [[characters/cloten\|Cloten]] a letter |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Let’s see’t. I will pursue her<br>Even to Augustus’ throne. |
| *(didascalia)* | PISANIO aside |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Or this or perish.<br>She’s far enough, and what he learns by this<br>May prove his travel, not her danger. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Hum! |
| PISANIO | (aside)<br>I’ll write to my lord she’s dead. O [[characters/innogen\|Innogen]],<br>Safe mayst thou wander, safe return again! |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Sirrah, is this letter true? |
| PISANIO | Sir, as I think. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | It is [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]]’ hand; I know’t. Sirrah, if thou wouldst not be a [[archetypes/villain\|villain]] but do me true service, undergo those employments wherein I should have cause to use thee with a serious industry—that is, what villainy soe’er I bid thee do, to perform it directly and truly—I would think thee an honest man. Thou shouldst neither want my means for thy relief nor my voice for thy preferment. |
| PISANIO | [[motifs/well\|Well]], my good lord. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Wilt thou serve me? For since patiently and constantly thou hast stuck to the bare fortune of that beggar [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]], thou canst not in the course of gratitude but be a diligent follower of mine. Wilt thou serve me? 121 |
| PISANIO | Sir, I will. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Give me thy hand. Here’s my purse. Hast any of thy late master’s garments in thy possession? |
| PISANIO | I have, my lord, at my lodging the same suit he wore when he took leave of my lady and mistress. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | The first service thou dost me, fetch that suit hither. Let it be thy first service. Go. |
| PISANIO | I shall, my lord. Exit |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Meet thee at Milford Haven! I forgot to ask him one thing; I’ll remember’t anon. Even there, thou [[archetypes/villain\|villain]] [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]], will I kill thee. I would these garments were come. She said upon a [[motifs/time\|time]]—the bitterness of it I now belch from my heart—that she held the very garment of [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]] in more respect than my noble and natural person, together with the adornment of my qualities. With that suit upon my back will I ravish her—first kill him, and in her eyes; there shall she see my valour, which will then be a torment to her contempt. He on the ground, my speech of insultment ended on his dead [[concepts/body\|body]], and when my lust hath dined—which, as I say, to vex her I will execute in the clothes that she so praised—to the [[settings/court\|court]] I’ll knock her back, foot her [[motifs/home\|home]] again. She hath despised me rejoicingly, and I’ll be merry in my [[concepts/revenge\|revenge]]. |
| *(didascalia)* | Enter Pisanio with [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]]’ suit |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Be those the garments? |
| PISANIO | Ay, my noble lord. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | How long is’t since she went to Milford Haven? |
| PISANIO | She can scarce be there yet. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Bring this apparel to my chamber. That is the second thing that I have commanded thee. The third is that thou wilt be a voluntary mute to my design. Be but duteous, and true preferment shall tender itself to thee. My [[concepts/revenge\|revenge]] is now at Milford. Would I had wings to follow it. Come, and be true. Exit |
| PISANIO | Thou bidd’st me to my loss, for true to thee<br>Were to prove false, which I will never be<br>To him that is most true. To Milford go,<br>And find not her whom thou pursuest. Flow, flow,<br>You heavenly blessings, on her. This [[archetypes/fool\|fool]]’s [[characters/speed\|speed]]<br>Be crossed with slowness; labour be his meed. Exit |

| *(didascalia)* | Fanfara. Entrano [[characters/cymbeline\|Cimbelino]], la [[characters/queen\|Regina]], [[characters/cloten\|Cloten]], [[characters/lucius\|Lucio]] e i lord |
| [[characters/cymbeline\|CIMBELINO]] | (a [[characters/lucius\|Lucio]])<br>Fin qui, e così addio. |
| [[characters/lucius\|LUCIO]] | Grazie, reale sire.<br>Il mio imperatore ha scritto che devo partire;<br>e sono assai dolente di dovervi chiamare<br>nemico del mio signore. |
| [[characters/cymbeline\|CIMBELINO]] | I nostri sudditi, signore,<br>non sopporteranno il suo giogo; e per noi<br>mostrar meno sovranità di quanto occorra<br>sarebbe indegno di un re. |
| [[characters/lucius\|LUCIO]] | Così, signore, io [[motifs/desire\|desidero]] da voi<br>una scorta per terra fino a Milford Haven. |
| [[characters/lucius\|LUCIO]] | (Alla [[characters/queen\|Regina]]) Signora, ogni gioia giunga alla vostra grazia, a [[characters/cloten\|Cloten]] e a voi. |
| [[characters/cymbeline\|CIMBELINO]] | Miei signori, siete stati designati per quell'ufficio.<br>Non tralasciate in alcun punto il debito dell'[[concepts/honour\|onore]].<br>Addio, nobile [[characters/lucius\|Lucio]]. |
| [[characters/lucius\|LUCIO]] | La vostra mano, mio signore. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | La riceva amichevolmente, ma da questo [[motifs/time\|tempo]] innanzi<br>la porto come vostro nemico. |
| [[characters/lucius\|LUCIO]] | Signore, l'esito<br>non ha ancora nominato il vincitore. State [[motifs/well\|bene]]. |
| [[characters/cymbeline\|CIMBELINO]] | Non lasciate il degno [[characters/lucius\|Lucio]], buoni miei signori,<br>finché non abbia attraversato il Severn. Felicità. |
| *(didascalia)* | Escono [[characters/lucius\|Lucio]] e i lord |
| [[characters/queen\|REGINA]] | Egli parte di qui accigliato, ma ci onora<br>che gli abbiamo dato motivo. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Tanto meglio.<br>I vostri valorosi Britanni in ciò vedono esauditi i loro desideri. |
| [[characters/cymbeline\|CIMBELINO]] | [[characters/lucius\|Lucio]] ha già scritto all'Imperatore<br>come qui vanno le cose. Ci conviene quindi, ormai,<br>che i nostri carri e i nostri cavalieri siano pronti.<br>Le forze che egli ha già in Gallia<br>saranno presto raccolte a capo, donde muove<br>la sua guerra per la Britannia. |
| [[characters/queen\|REGINA]] | Non è faccenda da dormire,<br>ma va seguita con prontezza e vigore. |
| [[characters/cymbeline\|CIMBELINO]] | La nostra attesa che così sarebbe stato<br>ci ha resi previdenti. Ma, mia dolce [[characters/queen\|regina]],<br>dov'è nostra figlia? Non è comparsa<br>davanti al Romano, né a noi ha reso<br>il dovere del giorno. Ci sembra<br>una cosa fatta più di malizia che di dovere.<br>L'abbiamo notato. Chiamatela davanti a noi, perché<br>siamo stati troppo indulgenti nel sopportare. |
| *(didascalia)* | Esce uno o più |
| [[characters/queen\|REGINA]] | Reale sire,<br>dall'[[concepts/exile\|esilio]] di [[characters/posthumus\|Postumo]] la sua vita<br>è stata assai ritirata; la cura di ciò, mio signore,<br>spetta al [[motifs/time\|tempo]]. Supplico vostra maestà<br>di trattenerla da parole aspre verso di lei. È una donna<br>così sensibile ai rimproveri che le parole sono colpi,<br>e i colpi [[motifs/death\|morte]] per lei. |
| *(didascalia)* | Entra un Messaggero |
| [[characters/cymbeline\|CIMBELINO]] | Dov'è, signore? Come<br>può giustificarsi il suo disprezzo? |
| MESSAGGERO | Compiaccia a voi, signore,<br>le sue stanze sono tutte chiuse, e non vi sarà risposta<br>al più forte rumore che facciamo. |
| [[characters/queen\|REGINA]] | Mio signore, quando ultimamente andai a visitarla<br>mi pregò di scusare il suo starsene rinchiusa,<br>dove costretta dalla sua infermità,<br>doveva lasciare non reso a voi quel dovere<br>che ogni giorno era tenuta a offrire. Questo<br>ella volle che vi facessi sapere, ma la nostra grande<br>[[settings/court\|corte]]<br>mi fece mancare in [[motifs/memory\|memoria]]. |
| [[characters/cymbeline\|CIMBELINO]] | Le sue porte chiuse?<br>Non vista da poco? Il cielo conceda che quel che<br>[[concepts/fear\|temo]] si mostri falso. |
| *(didascalia)* | Esce |
| [[characters/queen\|REGINA]] | Orsù, dico, seguite il [[archetypes/king\|re]]. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Quel suo uomo, Pisanio, il suo vecchio servo,<br>non l'ho visto da due giorni. |
| [[characters/queen\|REGINA]] | Va', cercalo. |
| *(didascalia)* | Esce [[characters/cloten\|Cloten]] |
| [[characters/queen\|REGINA]] | Pisanio, tu che tanto parteggi per [[characters/posthumus\|Postumo]]!<br>Egli ha una mia droga. Prego che la sua assenza<br>derivi dall'averla inghiottita, perché crede<br>che sia cosa preziosissima. Ma per lei,<br>dov'è andata? Forse la [[concepts/despair\|disperazione]] l'ha colta,<br>o, alata dall'ardore del suo [[motifs/love\|amore]], è volata<br>al suo desiderato [[characters/posthumus\|Postumo]]. È andata<br>verso la [[motifs/death\|morte]] o verso il disonore, e il mio fine<br>può trarre buon uso dall'uno e dall'altro. Con lei abbattuta,<br>spetta a me porre la britannica [[motifs/crown\|corona]]. |
| *(didascalia)* | Entra [[characters/cloten\|Cloten]] |
| [[characters/queen\|REGINA]] | Ebbene, figlio mio? |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | È certo che è fuggita.<br>Entra e rincuora il [[archetypes/king\|re]]. Infuria, nessuno<br>osa avvicinarglisi. |
| [[characters/queen\|REGINA]] | Tanto meglio. Possa<br>questa [[motifs/night\|notte]] defraudarlo del giorno che viene. Esce |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Io la [[motifs/love\|amo]] e la odio. Poiché è bella e regale,<br>e poiché ha tutte le doti di corte più squisite<br>di dama, dame, donna—da ciascuna<br>ha il meglio, e lei, composta di tutte,<br>le sopravanza tutte—per questo la [[motifs/love\|amo]]; ma<br>disprezzandomi e gettando i favori<br>sul vile [[characters/posthumus\|Postumo]], calunnia così il suo giudizio<br>che ogni altra rarità è soffocata; e su questo<br>concluderò per odiarla, anzi, davvero,<br>per vendicarmi di lei. Poiché quando gli stolti<br>— |
| *(didascalia)* | Entra Pisanio |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Chi è qui? Come, te ne vai, mascalzone?<br>Vieni qui. Ah, prezioso ruffiano! [[archetypes/villain\|Furfante]],<br>dov'è la tua signora? In una parola, o altrimenti<br>sei subito tra i diavoli. |
| PISANIO | O mio buon signore! |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Dov'è la tua signora?—o, per Giove,<br>non chiederò di nuovo. Subdolo [[archetypes/villain\|furfante]],<br>trarrò questo segreto dalla tua lingua o ti squarcerò<br>il cuore per trovarlo. È con [[characters/posthumus\|Postumo]],<br>dai cui tanti pesi di bassezza non può<br>trarsi un dramma di valore? |
| PISANIO | Ahimè, mio signore,<br>come può essere con lui? Quando fu notata la sua assenza?<br>Egli è a Roma. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Dov'è, signore? Fatti più vicino.<br>Basta indugi. Soddisfami [[motifs/home\|appieno]]<br>che ne è stato di lei. |
| PISANIO | O mio signore d'ogni valore! |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | [[archetypes/villain\|Furfante]] d'ogni valore,<br>scopri dov'è la tua signora all'istante,<br>alla prossima parola. Non più «degno signore».<br>Parla, o il tuo [[motifs/silence\|silenzio]] in un attimo è<br>la tua condanna e la tua [[motifs/death\|morte]]. |
| PISANIO | Allora, signore,<br>questa carta è la [[concepts/history\|storia]] di quanto so<br>intorno alla sua fuga.<br>Dà a [[characters/cloten\|Cloten]] una lettera |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Vediamo. La inseguirò<br>fin sul trono d'Augusto. |
| *(didascalia)* | PISANIO a parte |
| PISANIO | O questo o perire.<br>Ella è abbastanza lontana, e ciò che egli apprende da questo<br>può giovare al suo viaggio, non al suo pericolo. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Uhm! |
| PISANIO | (a parte)<br>Scriverò al mio signore ch'ella è morta. O [[characters/innogen\|Innogen]],<br>possa tu errare salva, salva far ritorno! |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Mascalzone, è vera questa lettera? |
| PISANIO | Signore, credo di sì. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | È la mano di [[characters/posthumus\|Postumo]]; la riconosco. Mascalzone, se non volessi essere un [[archetypes/villain\|furfante]] ma rendermi vero servizio, intraprendere quegli incarichi in cui avessi motivo di servirmi di te con seria diligenza—vale a dire, qualunque scelleratezza io ti ordini di fare, eseguirla direttamente e fedelmente—ti riterrei un onest'uomo. Non ti mancherebbero né i miei mezzi per il tuo sollievo, né la mia voce per il tuo avanzamento. |
| PISANIO | [[motifs/well\|Ebbene]], mio buon signore. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Mi servirai? Poiché con pazienza e costanza ti sei attaccato alla nuda fortuna di quel mendico [[characters/posthumus\|Postumo]], non puoi, per legge di gratitudine, non essere un diligente seguace mio. Mi servirai? 121 |
| PISANIO | Signore, sì. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Dammi la mano. Ecco la mia borsa. Hai in tuo possesso qualche vestito del tuo antico padrone? |
| PISANIO | Ne ho, mio signore, nel mio alloggio, lo stesso abito che indossava quando prese congedo dalla mia signora e padrona. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Il primo servizio che mi rendi è portare qui quell'abito. Sia il tuo primo servizio. Va'. |
| PISANIO | Lo farò, mio signore. Esce |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | T'incontrerò a Milford Haven! Ho dimenticato di chiedergli una cosa; me ne ricorderò tra poco. Proprio lì, [[archetypes/villain\|furfante]] [[characters/posthumus\|Postumo]], ti ucciderò. Vorrei che questi abiti fossero giunti. Ella disse una [[motifs/time\|volta]]—l'amarezza di ciò ora la rutto dal cuore—che teneva il medesimo abito di [[characters/posthumus\|Postumo]] in maggior rispetto che non la mia nobile e naturale persona, insieme con l'adornamento delle mie qualità. Con quell'abito addosso la violenterò—prima ucciderò lui, e davanti ai suoi occhi; lì ella vedrà il mio valore, che allora sarà un tormento per il suo disprezzo. Lui a terra, finito il mio discorso d'insulti sul suo morto [[concepts/body\|corpo]], e quando la mia libidine avrà desinato—che, come dico, per tormentarla compirò con gli abiti che tanto lodò—la ricaccerò indietro alla [[settings/court\|corte]], la riporterò [[motifs/home\|a casa]] a pedate. Ella mi ha disprezzato gioiosamente, e io sarò lieto nella mia [[concepts/revenge\|vendetta]]. |
| *(didascalia)* | Entra Pisanio con l'abito di [[characters/posthumus\|Postumo]] |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Sono quelli gli abiti? |
| PISANIO | Sì, mio nobile signore. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Quanto è passato da quando è andata a Milford Haven? |
| PISANIO | Non può ancora esserci arrivata. |
| [[characters/cloten\|CLOTEN]] | Porta questi abiti nella mia camera. Questa è la seconda cosa che ti ho comandato. La terza è che tu sia un muto volontario al mio disegno. Sii soltanto ubbidiente, e il vero avanzamento ti si offrirà da sé. La mia [[concepts/revenge\|vendetta]] è ora a Milford. Magari avessi ali per seguirla. Vieni, e sii fedele. Esce |
| PISANIO | Mi comandi a mia rovina, perché esser vero a te<br>sarebbe mostrarmi falso, cosa che non sarò mai<br>con colui che è il più vero. Va' a Milford,<br>e non trovare colei che insegui. Scorrete, scorrete,<br>voi benedizioni celesti, su di lei. La [[characters/speed\|fretta]] di questo [[archetypes/fool\|stolto]]<br>sia contrastata dalla lentezza; la fatica sia il suo premio. Esce |



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="act_3--scene_6" data-title="Cymbeline — Act III, Scene 6" data-chapter="Scene 6" data-kind="scene" data-tags="motif/cave,motif/love,motif/nature,motif/night,motif/pain,motif/well,concept/conscience,concept/fear,concept/nature,concept/truth,concept/wonder,setting/court,setting/italy,character/arviragus,character/belarius,character/cymbeline,character/guiderius,character/innogen,character/posthumus"></span>

| *(didascalia)* | Enter [[characters/innogen\|Innogen]], dressed as a man, before the [[motifs/cave\|cave]] |
| [[characters/innogen\|INNOGEN]] | I see a man’s life is a tedious one.<br>I have tired myself, and for two nights together<br>Have made the ground my bed. I should be sick,<br>But that my resolution helps me. Milford,<br>When from the mountain-top Pisanio showed thee,<br>Thou wast within a ken. O Jove, I think<br>Foundations fly the wretched—such, I mean,<br>Where they should be relieved. Two beggars told me<br>I could not miss my way. Will poor folks lie,<br>That have afflictions on them, knowing ‘tis<br>A punishment or trial? Yes. No [[concepts/wonder\|wonder]],<br>When rich ones scarce tell true. To lapse in fullness<br>Is sorer than to lie for need, and falsehood<br>Is worse in kings than beggars. My dear lord,<br>Thou art one o’th’ false ones. Now I think on thee<br>My hunger’s gone, but even before I was<br>At point to sink for food. But what is this?<br>Here is a path to’t. ‘Tis some savage hold.<br>I were best not call; I dare not call; yet famine,<br>Ere clean it o’erthrow [[concepts/nature\|nature]], makes it valiant.<br>Plenty and peace breeds cowards, hardness ever<br>Of hardiness is mother. Ho! Who’s here?<br>If anything that’s civil, speak; if savage,<br>Take or lend. Ho! No answer? Then I’ll enter.<br>Best draw my sword, and if mine enemy<br>But [[concepts/fear\|fear]] the sword like me he’ll scarcely look on’t.<br>Such a foe, good heavens! |
| *(didascalia)* | Exit into the [[motifs/cave\|cave]] |
| *(didascalia)* | Enter [[characters/belarius\|Belarius]], [[characters/guiderius\|Guiderius]], and [[characters/arviragus\|Arviragus]] |
| [[characters/belarius\|BELARIUS]] | You, Polydore, have proved best woodman and<br>Are master of the feast. Cadwal and I<br>Will play the cook and servant; ‘tis our match.<br>The sweat of industry would dry and die<br>But for the end it works to. Come, our stomachs<br>Will make what’s homely savoury. Weariness<br>Can snore upon the flint when resty sloth<br>Finds the down pillow hard. Now peace be here,<br>Poor house, that keep’st thyself. |
| [[characters/guiderius\|GUIDERIUS]] | I am throughly weary. |
| [[characters/arviragus\|ARVIRAGUS]] | I am weak with toil yet strong in appetite. |
| [[characters/guiderius\|GUIDERIUS]] | There is cold meat i’th’ [[motifs/cave\|cave]]. We’ll browse on that<br>Whilst what we have killed be cooked. |
| [[characters/belarius\|BELARIUS]] | (looking into the [[motifs/cave\|cave]]) Stay, come not in.<br>But that it eats our victuals I should think<br>Here were a fairy. |
| [[characters/guiderius\|GUIDERIUS]] | What’s the matter, sir? |
| [[characters/belarius\|BELARIUS]] | By Jupiter, an angel—or, if not,<br>An earthly paragon. Behold divineness<br>No elder than a boy. |
| *(didascalia)* | Enter [[characters/innogen\|Innogen]] from the [[motifs/cave\|cave]], dressed as a man |
| [[characters/innogen\|INNOGEN]] | Good masters, harm me not.<br>Before I entered here I called, and thought<br>To have begged or bought what I have took. Good<br>[[concepts/truth\|truth]],<br>I have stol’n naught, nor would not, though I had<br>found<br>Gold strewed i’th’ floor. Here’s money for my meat.<br>I would have left it on the board so soon<br>As I had made my meal, and parted<br>With prayers for the provider. |
| [[characters/guiderius\|GUIDERIUS]] | Money, youth? |
| [[characters/arviragus\|ARVIRAGUS]] | All gold and silver rather turn to dirt,<br>As ’tis no better reckoned but of those<br>Who worship dirty gods. |
| [[characters/innogen\|INNOGEN]] | I see you’re angry.<br>Know, if you kill me for my fault, I should<br>Have died had I not made it. |
| [[characters/belarius\|BELARIUS]] | Whither bound? |
| [[characters/innogen\|INNOGEN]] | To Milford Haven. |
| [[characters/belarius\|BELARIUS]] | What’s your name? |
| [[characters/innogen\|INNOGEN]] | Fidele, sir. I have a kinsman who<br>Is bound for [[settings/italy\|Italy]]. He embarked at Milford,<br>To whom being going, almost spent with hunger,<br>I am fall’n in this offence. |
| [[characters/belarius\|BELARIUS]] | Prithee, fair youth,<br>Think us no churls, nor measure our good minds<br>By this rude place we live in. [[motifs/well\|Well]] encountered.<br>’Tis almost [[motifs/night\|night]]. You shall have better cheer<br>Ere you depart, and thanks to stay and eat it.<br>Boys, bid him welcome. |
| [[characters/guiderius\|GUIDERIUS]] | Were you a woman, youth,<br>I should woo hard but be your groom in honesty,<br>Ay, bid for you as I’d buy. |
| [[characters/arviragus\|ARVIRAGUS]] | I’ll make’t my comfort<br>He is a man, I’ll [[motifs/love\|love]] him as my brother.<br>(To [[characters/innogen\|Innogen]]) And such a welcome as I’d give to him<br>After long absence, such is yours. Most welcome.<br>Be sprightly, for you fall ’mongst friends. |
| [[characters/innogen\|INNOGEN]] | ’Mongst friends<br>If brothers. (Aside) Would it had been so that they<br>Had been my father’s sons. Then had my price<br>Been less, and so more equal ballasting<br>To thee, [[characters/posthumus\|Posthumus]].<br>The three men speak apart |
| [[characters/belarius\|BELARIUS]] | He wrings at some distress. |
| [[characters/guiderius\|GUIDERIUS]] | Would I could free’t. |
| [[characters/arviragus\|ARVIRAGUS]] | Or I, whate’er it be,<br>What [[motifs/pain\|pain]] it cost, what danger. Gods! |
| [[characters/belarius\|BELARIUS]] | Hark, boys.<br>They whisper |
| [[characters/innogen\|INNOGEN]] | (aside) Great men<br>That had a [[settings/court\|court]] no bigger than this [[motifs/cave\|cave]],<br>That did attend themselves and had the virtue<br>Which their own [[concepts/conscience\|conscience]] sealed them, laying by<br>That nothing-gift of differing multitudes,<br>Could not outpeer these twain. Pardon me, gods,<br>I’d change my sex to be companion with them,<br>Since Leonatus’ false. |
| [[characters/belarius\|BELARIUS]] | It shall be so.<br>Boys, we’ll go dress our hunt. Fair youth, come in.<br>Discourse is heavy, fasting. When we have supped<br>We’ll mannerly demand thee of thy story,<br>So far as thou wilt speak it. |
| [[characters/guiderius\|GUIDERIUS]] | Pray draw near. |
| [[characters/arviragus\|ARVIRAGUS]] | The [[motifs/night\|night]] to th’ owl and morn to th’ lark less welcome. |
| [[characters/innogen\|INNOGEN]] | Thanks, sir. |
| [[characters/arviragus\|ARVIRAGUS]] | I pray draw near. |
| *(didascalia)* | Exeunt into the [[motifs/cave\|cave]] |
